the interactive session (#12)

* fix(audit): reject absent platform evidence

* fix(audit): close absent evidence gaps

* refactor(audit): simplify branch rule decoding

* feat(tui): the interactive console shell

Bare `airlock` on an interactive terminal opens the release-readiness
console. It has no subcommand and no flag, so an agent holding this
binary has nothing to invoke: the boundary is the absence of the code
path rather than a check declining to take it.

Off a terminal — pipe, redirect, or scheduler — it exits non-zero
before rendering anything, and names the unattended surfaces to run
instead.

The shell is the frame every later screen sits in:

* the status-lane primitive, implemented once — nine statuses, one
  glyph each, three lanes, and the undecided lane fenced on both sides
  of every row so nothing standing in it reads as a pass;
* both palettes, switchable with `t`, and `NO_COLOR` collapsing every
  role to the terminal's own colours without losing a distinction;
* header, breadcrumb, keymap footer, and status line, degrading from
  the 120x40 reference to the 80x24 floor by giving rows back to the
  body and eliding rather than clipping;
* navigation between the eight screens, each stating what would have
  populated it and why it is empty;
* the terminal restored on the clean, error, panic, and signal paths.

Rendering is recorded as snapshots of the character grid and a
per-cell style grid, at both sizes, in both palettes, and under
`NO_COLOR`.

ratatui 0.30 with the crossterm backend draws it. Both are pure Rust
with no C dependency, ratatui declares exactly our 1.86 MSRV, and its
`TestBackend` renders into a comparable buffer, which is what makes
the frame provable without a terminal.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015KHqogouHqTDH1ZcnJnTRb

* fix(tui): close the terminal acquisition gap and prove restoration

Taking the terminal is several fallible calls, and the first of them
already changes it. A failure in any of the later ones returned an
error over a terminal left in raw mode, on the alternate screen, with
no cursor: the operator's shell, broken, with only an error message to
explain it.

The restorer is now armed before the first call that changes anything,
so every way out after that point — `?`, panic, or a clean return —
unwinds through it. The acquisition sequence moves behind a seam so
the ordering itself is testable with an injected failure rather than
inferred from reading it.

Restoration is also now proven rather than asserted. A new suite drives
the binary through a real pseudo-terminal in a real child process and
checks the line discipline read back off the pty after the child is
gone — not the escape bytes alone, because a program can print the
right sequence and still leave the terminal raw. It covers a clean
exit, a delivered signal (terminal restored, and the process still
dies of signal 2 so the exit status still says what killed it), and a
refusal off a terminal touching nothing at all.

The panic path is asserted where the panic can be raised directly.
Reaching it from outside the binary would need a failure-injection
hook in a shipped surface, which is a worse trade than covering it
in place; the suite says so and says why.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015KHqogouHqTDH1ZcnJnTRb

* feat(tui): sign-in, the device flow, and the write credential

The console now acquires its own authorization. Bare `airlock` runs the
GitHub App device flow and draws all five states the terminal interface
specification names — requesting a code, awaiting approval with a live
poll count and remaining validity, expired, denied, and polling
interrupted. Each names its remedy.

Expiry and denial issue a replacement code in place: the session is not
restarted and nothing else is lost, because nothing else lives on this
screen. An interruption keeps the still-valid code with what is left of
its validity and shows its backoff, so approval already given is picked
up when polling resumes rather than wasted. A denial states plainly that
nothing was granted and there is no credential to revoke.

The scan code is an accelerator only. It encodes the address, because
the device flow offers no address that carries the code, so the code is
always typed and is always legible text — spaced character by character,
over an alphabet that already excludes 0, O, 1, and I. It paints its own
white field and four-module quiet zone rather than inheriting the
terminal background, so it scans the same on both palettes. It is
withheld rather than clipped whenever it cannot be drawn whole: too
narrow, too short, or `NO_COLOR`, each said by name, with `q` to draw it
below the code instead.

The whole screen fits the 80x24 floor, credential statement included. It
says the same things in fewer words there rather than saying some of
them and letting the frame withhold the rest.

The credential:

* has one source, structurally — the type that holds it can be built
  from nothing but a device grant, so there is no flag, no environment
  variable, and no config entry to remove;
* is never stored, never exported to a child process, never displayed,
  and is overwritten when it goes;
* keeps no refresh token: GitHub sends one, and it is zeroized on
  arrival;
* lives in the run loop rather than in the drawing state, so what
  renders the screen cannot reach it.

The accepted app is a compile-time constant, bound by both numeric id
and slug — an id survives a rename and a slug does not. A build with
`--features test-identity` accepts Airlock Test, installed on one
account only; the shipped binary accepts Airlock Admin and contains no
string that could accept anything else. That is asserted against the
built artifact, not against a configuration value.

The flow runs on its own thread with its own runtime and speaks to the
loop over channels, so a 30-second request timeout cannot stop the
countdown on screen. The device code airlock polls with never crosses
that channel.

The OAuth host override the suite needs is honoured only for a loopback
address. A general override would be a way to redirect where an
operator's approval goes, which is what binding the identity prevents.

Tests cover each state, the storage prohibitions as source-level
absences, the binding against the built binary, and a whole session
under a pseudo-terminal with every writable directory redirected into
one watched place, which stays empty.

* fix(tui): close four findings on the write credential path

Cross-review found four security defects and one overclaim. Each fix
carries a test that fails against the code as it was.

**The loopback check was a prefix test.** `http://localhost:80@attacker
.example` passed it, because the authority was split on its last colon
and the userinfo before the `@` was read as the host — so an environment
variable could send an operator's approval to a host of someone else's
choosing, which is the one thing binding the identity at compile time
exists to prevent. The authority is now taken apart rather than matched
against: userinfo is refused outright, a bracketed IPv6 literal must
close and be followed by nothing or a port, a port must be digits, and
the host must equal a loopback name rather than begin with one. The
refusals are enumerated in the test, the finding's own URL among them.

**The grant reached the type that draws.** `App::report` took the
worker's `Report`, which has a `Granted` arm, so the design's central
claim was true only by convention: the drawing state was handed a
credential and immediately gave it back. The worker's messages are now
split. `Progress` is what the interface is given and has no arm that
could carry a credential; `Report` adds the one that does, and the run
loop takes it apart before `App` is told anything. `App` is told that an
authorization exists, never what it is, and its signatures name no type
that could carry one.

The same split removed a second leak the module doc had already claimed
was closed: `CodeIssued` carried the whole device-code response,
including the code airlock polls with. What crosses now is `Issued`,
which has no field for it.

**Shutdown detached the worker.** A grant queued and unread, or acquired
after the session had gone, was left in a freed allocation on a thread
nobody was waiting for. Three changes, and all three are needed:
`TokenGrant` now zeroizes on drop, so the guarantee belongs to the value
rather than to where it happens to be; the request channel is a tokio
one and every await on the worker selects against it, so closing it
abandons an in-flight poll rather than running out a thirty-second
timeout; and shutdown is ordered — close, drain, join, drain — so a
grant sent during the join is cleared too. A test drops the session
against a server that stalls for twenty seconds and asserts the drop
returns inside its budget.

**Server text reached the terminal unexamined.** A terminal is an
interpreter, so a code, an address, or an error description GitHub chose
was a program for it: clear the screen, retitle the window, or move the
cursor over the statement that no credential is stored — and a
bidirectional override could make an address read as one host and
resolve as another, including through the address the scan code
encodes. `admin::text::sanitize` replaces control characters, C1, and
the bidirectional and zero-width format characters, and bounds length.
It is applied where server data leaves the worker, and again in the
state the screen renders, so the state machine's guarantee does not
depend on which caller it has. A test renders both states that carry
server text, in every scan-code placement and at both sizes, and reads
every cell.

**The negative-evidence tests claimed more than they showed.** The
session test now also watches the working directory and the rest of the
temporary-directory variables, and both it and the source scans say what
they prove and what they do not: the identity binding and the credential
type's shape are read out of the artifact and the declaration and are
proofs; the source scans catch a reintroduction under today's names and
are tripwires. The README's claim is narrowed to match, and gains the
sanitization guarantee and the fact that the interface is never given
the credential at all.

The snapshot comparison is skipped under `--features test-identity`,
which names Airlock Test on screen; that build asserts it says so
instead.

* fix(tui): validate the OAuth host with the client's own URL parser

The hand-written authority check that replaced the string-prefix one was
still a second reading of a URL, and a second reading is a second thing
to be wrong. `url::Url` — the crate reqwest resolves with — now does the
parsing, so what is validated and what is dialled cannot disagree.

Userinfo, a query, a fragment, and a path are all refused rather than
parsed past, and the host must be a loopback address or exactly
`localhost` after the parser has normalised it. A base carrying its own
path is refused too: it is concatenated with one, so it would not mean
what it reads as.

The scan code now checks the address's shape as well as its characters.
A scanner that followed a code airlock drew would go wherever it
pointed, so an address that is not an `http` or `https` URL is printed
and not encoded, and the screen says why — reading it is the operator's,
and following it is not something this screen offers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015KHqogouHqTDH1ZcnJnTRb

* fix(tui): encode a scan code only for the origin airlock asked

Verification found the residual hole in the previous fix: the scan code
checked that the address looked like a link, not that it was the right
one, so a hostile response carrying `https://attacker.example` was still
encoded. Looking like a web address was never the test — that is exactly
what an attacker's address does. A scan code is followed without being
read, which is the whole of what it is for, so the destination must not
be the server's to choose.

`text::is_at_origin` replaces `is_web_address`. An address is encodable
only when its origin equals the origin airlock sent its own request to,
which `flow::login_origin` derives from the base actually used — GitHub
in a shipped run, and the validated loopback origin when the suite has
pointed the flow at its own server. Deriving it rather than writing it
down twice is what keeps the host that was dialled and the host a
scanner can be sent to from drifting apart. An origin that cannot be
read serialises to `null` and matches nothing, so the check fails
closed.

The comparison is on origin rather than on the whole address: a path is
GitHub's to change, and an attacker who can already choose a path on
`github.com` gains nothing from a scan code. A mismatched address is
still printed as the text it is — reading it is the operator's, and
hiding it would not help them — and the screen names the origin it
expected.

Writing the regression test found a second defect underneath. The
layout took the symbol's size from a constant, so a longer address —
`.../device/somewhere-else` needs 37 columns rather than 33 — would have
been drawn past the column reserved for it and off the edge of the
terminal, which is precisely the clipping the withholding rule exists to
prevent. The placement now measures the symbol it is about to draw and
carries it, so the size the layout was decided against and the size that
is painted are the same one. The withheld reasons report the actual
requirement rather than the budget. The 33-column figure remains as the
specification's budget for the expected address and as the threshold the

**The loopback check was a prefix test.** `http://localhost:80@attacker
.example` passed it, because the authority was split on its last colon
and the userinfo before the `@` was read as the host — so an environment
variable could send an operator's approval to a host of someone else's
choosing, which is the one thing binding the identity at compile time
exists to prevent. The authority is now taken apart rather than matched
against: userinfo is refused outright, a bracketed IPv6 literal must
close and be followed by nothing or a port, a port must be digits, and
the host must equal a loopback name rather than begin with one. The
refusals are enumerated in the test, the finding's own URL among them.

**The grant reached the type that draws.** `App::report` took the
worker's `Report`, which has a `Granted` arm, so the design's central
claim was true only by convention: the drawing state was handed a
credential and immediately gave it back. The worker's messages are now
split. `Progress` is what the interface is given and has no arm that
could carry a credential; `Report` adds the one that does, and the run
loop takes it apart before `App` is told anything. `App` is told that an
authorization exists, never what it is, and its signatures name no type
that could carry one.

The same split removed a second leak the module doc had already claimed
was closed: `CodeIssued` carried the whole device-code response,
including the code airlock polls with. What crosses now is `Issued`,
which has no field for it.

**Shutdown detached the worker.** A grant queued and unread, or acquired
after the session had gone, was left in a freed allocation on a thread
nobody was waiting for. Three changes, and all three are needed:
`TokenGrant` now zeroizes on drop, so the guarantee belongs to the value
rather than to where it happens to be; the request channel is a tokio
one and every await on the worker selects against it, so closing it
abandons an in-flight poll rather than running out a thirty-second
timeout; and shutdown is ordered — close, drain, join, drain — so a
grant sent during the join is cleared too. A test drops the session
against a server that stalls for twenty seconds and asserts the drop
returns inside its budget.

**Server text reached the terminal unexamined.** A terminal is an
interpreter, so a code, an address, or an error description GitHub chose
was a program for it: clear the screen, retitle the window, or move the
cursor over the statement that no credential is stored — and a
bidirectional override could make an address read as one host and
resolve as another, including through the address the scan code
encodes. `admin::text::sanitize` replaces control characters, C1, and
the bidirectional and zero-width format characters, and bounds length.
It is applied where server data leaves the worker, and again in the
state the screen renders, so the state machine's guarantee does not
depend on which caller it has. A test renders both states that carry
server text, in every scan-code placement and at both sizes, and reads
every cell.

session test now also watches the working directory and the rest of the
temporary-directory variables, and both it and the source scans say what
they prove and what they do not: the identity binding and the credential
type's shape are read out of the artifact and the declaration and are
proofs; the source scans catch a reintroduction under today's names and

sanitization guarantee and the fact that the interface is never given
the credential at all.

its grant in its scope list and presents an empty installation list, so it
resolved to `ReadOnly` on an unread grant — and `ReadOnly` is the answer that
lets a rule's declared disclosure gate retire a gap as permanent. The
interactive session authorises per launch through the device flow, which is
exactly the scoped shape, so the one path that must not inherit the audit's
exemption was the path that would have.

Both representations are now read, and a scope the reviewed read-only list does
not name counts as a write — the rule `verify_scoped` already applies when
admitting a token, asked of the capability instead of of admission. An empty
scope list stays `ReadOnly`, because GitHub stating that a token holds no scopes
is an enumerated answer rather than a missing one. A grant with no readable
representation at all resolves to `WriteCapable`.

The asymmetry is now stated where the type is declared: mislabelling a
write-capable credential read-only excuses a field it should have been shown and
retires a real gap, while mislabelling a read-only one write-capable only
overstates what a retry can achieve. Uncertainty therefore resolves to
write-capable, and a circumstantial inconclusive is the honest result.

its gap takes: a remediation with a stable code, the change it would
make, whether it is reversible, and its lane — deterministic file
change, judgment file change, or operator-only setting — or an explicit
no-remediation reason. A test holds the classification table and the
registry to the same rules in the same order, so a rule cannot be
registered without being classified.

Findings carry the declaration in a new always-present
remediation_class field, joined centrally from the rule id; no check
supplies a lane. The classification stays outside the registry digest:
the digest attests what rules mean, and a better answer to a gap must
not invalidate policy compatibility.

Every rule states, as data next to its identity, whether it reads the
repository's file tree or platform state only the GitHub API reports.
The domain is declared per rule and read everywhere; like remediation

* feat: observe file-level rules from a local working tree

File-level checks now read through the same snapshot from either of two
sources: the API tree, or a working tree on disk — one check, two
sources. The working tree is observed as it stands, uncommitted and
untracked content included; gitignored files are excluded (tracked
files are still read), and git facts come from gix in-process — the
binary still never shells out.

Every finding records which source decided it, and the report carries
an observation block stating the run's terms: file and platform
sources, the working tree's HEAD, and whether it was dirty (untracked
and deleted files count; undetermined is never reported clean). A
mixed run keeps platform rules on the API; a credential-less run gates
them to inconclusive `not_observed` before any check could read
synthesized state — never passing. An unreadable local path is a new
file state that checks report as inconclusive.

`airlock audit owner/repo --working-tree .` mixes sources;
`airlock audit --working-tree . --policy ./policy.yml` runs local-only
against the new offline client and needs no credential. Airlock still
never requires a clone.

labels, the not-observed gating of platform rules, dirty and clean
reporting, ignored-file exclusion, untracked inclusion, and refusal of
a directory that is not a git repository. README documents the two
sources and what a mixed run means.

the airlock audit — policy-driven release-readiness findings (#1)

* feat: scaffold airlock cargo workspace

Two-crate workspace following the Wyrd Rust CLI convention: airlock-core for
checks, policy, findings, and the GitHub client, and airlock-cli for the
`airlock` binary.

The command surface (audit, auth login, auth status) is declared in full and
exits 2 as unimplemented. Bare invocation is implemented for real: there is no
interactive mode, so it reports that and exits 2 either way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* ci: add repository standards scaffolding

Mechanical files from the repository-standards templates, adapted to a Rust
workspace: line-ending and lockfile attributes, editor settings, the org
Renovate preset, lefthook hooks, the taskfile, CI, and declared repository
settings with their reconcile workflow.

Every action is pinned to a resolved commit SHA. go-task/setup-task pins to v2,
its newest release; the template's v3 does not exist yet.

CI adds a job pinned to the declared minimum supported Rust version, so
rust-version in Cargo.toml is enforced rather than asserted.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: add readme, agent guidance, and release configuration

README, AGENTS.md with CLAUDE.md symlinked to it, and CONTRIBUTING.md, written
for what airlock is rather than what the scaffold produced.

.intentional/config.yml declares airlock as a single release unit and projects
the computed version onto the workspace manifest and the cli-to-core dependency
pin, so the two cannot drift. CHANGELOG.md is the empty skeleton those releases
will fill.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* chore: add rust devcontainer

Minimal Rust container with a cargo cache volume, matching the pattern tagver
uses, plus the Task feature so `task check` works on first open.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(core): add hardened yaml loading, budgets, and the github client

Everything airlock parses comes from a repository it does not control, so
the YAML loader materialises documents into a closed value type under an
explicit budget and refuses tags, non-string keys, duplicate keys, deep
nesting, and alias expansion bombs.

The GitHub client is read-only by construction and classifies failures once,
from stable signals first: status, rate-limit headers, Retry-After, and
X-Accepted-GitHub-Permissions decide before a versioned table of message
hints is consulted, so GitHub's prose is never the deciding evidence.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(core): compile the conformance checklist into a versioned registry

All 109 rules are registered with statements copied verbatim from the
conformance checklist, their documented severity, and an evaluation mode.
Judgment rules are registered manual, rules not yet built are registered
unimplemented, so a policy that enables one gets a visible result rather
than a silently narrower audit.

A test parses a committed copy of the checklist and fails on drift in
either direction, and the registry carries a content digest over the sorted
(id, statement, severity, evaluation) tuples so two binaries that agree on
the digest agree on what every rule means.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(core): verify credentials by positive enumeration

A token is accepted only when its whole grant can be listed and every entry
is a read. Airlock Safe app user tokens are verified against the issuing app
GitHub attests on every installation, across every page; classic and OAuth
tokens against a closed allowlist of scopes whose full authority is
read-only. Fine-grained tokens, installation tokens, unknown prefixes, and a
missing scope header are refused as unverifiable rather than assumed safe.

The findings document carries the completeness model: eight statuses, a gate
over severities, and top-level complete/conformant/outcome, so an audit that
did not decide a gate-relevant rule exits 2 instead of reporting success.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(core): resolve, pin, and normalise policies

A policy resolves from the owner's .github repository, an explicit
owner/repo:path[@ref], or a local file, and every transitive reference is
pinned to a commit or a content hash before anything runs. The bundle digest
covers the sources and the compiled rule instances, so an audit names the
exact inputs that produced it.

Normalisation is deterministic and closed: capabilities select sections,
checks entries refine them, enabled:false always wins, and an unknown key,
section, rule, parameter, severity, or condition is a policy error rather
than a silently narrower audit. Suppression authority lives in the policy;
the audited repository may only request.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(core): implement the checks and the audit run

Checks read a single repository snapshot taken at one resolved commit, with
live settings recorded as a second domain stamped with when they were seen.
A check never reports pass for an assertion it did not fully evaluate: a
bounded history scan that hit its budget is inconclusive with the bound in
evidence, a rule whose remaining clause is judgment is manual, and an
unreadable file is undecided rather than absent.

The audit run compiles the effective policy, produces exactly one finding
per enabled rule, applies suppressions only to failures, and records a
repository's unauthorised suppression requests as observations rather than
letting them change any finding.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(cli): wire the audit, credential storage, and the device flow

The binary resolves a credential from --token, --token-file, --token-stdin,
AIRLOCK_TOKEN, then the stored profile, and nothing else — not GH_TOKEN, not
GITHUB_TOKEN, not the gh credential store, and it never hints they exist.
Every token is verified read-only before the first audit request.

Stored credentials are treated as secrets from the first syscall: created
0600, replaced by an atomic rename, refused if the file is a symlink or
readable by anyone but its owner, and rotated under a lock because a refresh
invalidates both previous tokens the moment it succeeds.

End-to-end tests run the real binary against a fixture GitHub covering the
conformant, nonconformant, incomplete, plan-limited, suppressed, and
adversarial-YAML paths.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat: add the dogfood job, the candidate org policy, and the audit docs

Airlock audits airlock in CI. The job is present before the credential is:
the audit step is skipped until an operator provisions AIRLOCK_TOKEN, so the
workflow says what it is and is not checking rather than failing every run.

The candidate wyrd-company policy and its topic vocabulary live in
docs/examples until the operator moves them into wyrd-company/.github. An
integration test compiles that policy against this binary's registry and
resolves its reference data, so a policy that would break dogfooding the
moment it moved breaks the build instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: point agent guidance at the registry and the examples tree

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): never conclude from a listing or tree airlock did not fully read

Paginated tag, ruleset, and branch-rule listings now carry whether the walk
stopped at the page budget, and every assertion over a whole collection
reports inconclusive when it did. A `v`-prefixed tag on page 21 no longer
lets REPO-GIT-08 pass, and an organisation ruleset outside the collected
prefix is no longer read as absent.

The same rule applies to the recursive tree. A path missing from a truncated
tree is undecided rather than absent, so REPO-FILE-13, REPO-FILE-14, the
dual-licence scan, and every presence check report inconclusive instead of
drawing a conclusion from state they never received.

Collection members are now decoded strictly. A tree entry, tag, commit,
ruleset, or branch rule airlock cannot read is a malformed response, never
one fewer item — a malformed `.claude/config` entry used to disappear and
help REPO-FILE-13 pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: bind the issuer, budget the clock, and refuse ambiguous headers

Airlock Safe app user tokens are now bound to both halves of GitHub's issuer
attestation: the immutable app id 4409712 as well as the slug. A renamed app,
a reused slug, or an installation reporting app id zero or no app id at all
is refused rather than trusted.

Response headers are kept multi-valued. Two `X-OAuth-Scopes` fields have no
combination rule airlock is willing to invent, so a response carrying both a
read-only value and `repo` is refused whichever order they arrive in, and two
Link headers are a malformed response rather than a coin toss over which page
to fetch next.

Every request now carries connect and read timeouts, response bodies are read
under a byte cap rather than buffered whole, the recursive tree is checked
against the declared entry budget, and the whole run carries a wall-clock
deadline. The client takes all of these from the audit's Limits instead of
inventing private defaults. Policy bundles spend one aggregate byte budget
across the root and every reference, so a blob that would exceed it is
refused before it is fetched.

REPO-CI-04 now requires a version comment that names a version: a bare `#`,
a whitespace-only comment, and a `#` inside a quoted scalar no longer pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close the three residual fail-open paths

A capability condition is now three-valued. `intentional-config-present`
asked `has_file`, which answers false for a path airlock never established
the absence of, so a truncated tree conclusively skipped every release rule
the registry capability governs. A condition whose input is truncated, over
budget, or unreadable now yields an inconclusive finding for each rule it
governs, and an audit that could not evaluate it is incomplete.

The device flow builds its own HTTP client, which had no timeouts at all —
so `auth login` and, through the refresh that runs before the bounded REST
client exists, `audit` and `auth status` could hang forever on a server that
accepted the connection and never answered. It now carries the same connect
and request timeouts as the audit path, reads bodies under a byte cap, and
bounds the whole poll loop to the lifetime of the device code it is polling
for.

Tag decoding no longer treats an unexpected ref as "simply not a tag". The
endpoint airlock asks is the refs/tags matching-ref collection, so a
refs/heads, refs/pull, or truncated refs/tag entry is malformed API data —
skipping it could empty a whole tag listing and let "no tag carries a `v`
prefix" pass over tags airlock never read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): report what each policy source pinned to, and read declarations whole

The bundle digest told a reviewer that the policy inputs changed without
telling them which reference changed, which is most of the value of pinning
reference data. Every source now carries its own resolved identity — commit
and blob sha for a remote source, content hash for a local one — through to
the findings document and the text renderer.

Sequences read out of files the audited repository controls are now read
strictly, through one shared helper. `topics: [cli, 42, rust]` used to yield
two topics: the count rule then failed a repository that declared three, and
the vocabulary rule never compared the dropped entry against the vocabulary
that would have rejected it. A wrong-typed entry is malformed input and the
rule reports it, in the same shape the GitHub client already uses for API
collections. The sweep covers topics, trigger lists, push branches, CD tag
patterns, renovate presets, branch-rule merge methods, hook commands, and the
policy's own topic vocabulary.

The text summary line is derived from the status taxonomy rather than
restating its eight members, so a ninth status cannot be added without the
renderer following.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): keep error causes and model credential selection truthfully

`main` prints `{error:#}`, which walks the source chain — but every core
error was being flattened into a fresh anyhow message first, so the chain it
walked was one link long. Each boundary now converts through `?` with a
`context` naming what airlock was trying to do, and the underlying cause
survives to the terminal.

Credential selection and credential origin were the same enum, which left a
`RefreshedProfile` arm that `selected_source` could never return and a match
arm nothing could reach. They are two enums now: selection is decided before
anything is read and cannot know whether a refresh will be needed.

The `AIRLOCK_TOKEN` name is read from its constant rather than respelled as a
literal, and a target that clap guarantees is present is no longer defaulted
into an empty string that reported "`` is not a repository".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* chore: point the topic vocabulary at its real home and tidy the manifests

The declared settings pointed readers at references/topics.md, a path left
over from the repository-standards template that does not exist here. The
vocabulary lives in the org policy's reference data.

AGENTS.md widened the no-shelling-out rule to "the tooling around it" and then
narrowed it to the binary, which reads as a standing violation by the
reconcile workflow. It is a rule about the binary; a workflow holding a scoped
token is exactly where a write belongs.

Both dev-dependency blocks restated tokio's features, which the workspace
already declares.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: read policy list parameters strictly and finish the error-cause sweep

`org-names: [wyrd-company, 42]` silently dropped an entry, so the rule that
forbids an organisation-name topic could pass while checking against a
shorter list than the policy declared. A list parameter that is not a list of
strings is now a malformed parameter the rule reports, naming the position of
the entry airlock could not read.

The last two boundaries in `auth login` were still flattening core errors
into fresh anyhow messages, dropping the source chain `main` prints, and one
test respelled AIRLOCK_TOKEN instead of using the constant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): make the two scope-header answers a type, and test the tree branch

`X-OAuth-Scopes` has three answers — absent, present-and-possibly-empty, and
repeated — and a Vec collapsed the first two into shapes a reader had to
decode, with a redundant boolean beside it that verification discarded. They
are an enum now, so each case is named where it is decided: an absent header
is an unread grant and refused, a present-but-empty header is GitHub stating
the token holds no scopes and is accepted, with the reasoning written where
the decision is made rather than inferred from a slice pattern.

The truncated-tree snapshot test reimplemented the production branch instead
of asserting through `file()`, so it passed whatever that branch did. It now
asserts through the accessor every check uses, in both directions; inverting
the branch fails four tests where it previously failed none.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: raise the minimum supported Rust version to 1.86

The dependency tree requires it: the icu_* crates that idna (via
reqwest's url) resolves to declare rustc 1.86, so a 1.85 toolchain
cannot even resolve the lockfile. Only CI's pinned MSRV job catches
this; the local msrv task runs on the installed toolchain.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: scope the msrv gate to what consumers build

The minimum supported Rust version is a promise about building airlock,
not about running its test suite; wiremock (dev-only) needs 1.88 without
declaring it, and it has no business setting the published floor. The
full suite still runs on stable in the test job.

The candidate wyrd-company policy and its topic vocabulary live in
docs/examples until the operator moves them into wyrd-company/.github. An
integration test compiles that policy against this binary's registry and
resolves its reference data, so a policy that would break dogfooding the
moment it moved breaks the build instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs: point agent guidance at the registry and the examples tree

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): never conclude from a listing or tree airlock did not fully read

Paginated tag, ruleset, and branch-rule listings now carry whether the walk
stopped at the page budget, and every assertion over a whole collection
reports inconclusive when it did. A `v`-prefixed tag on page 21 no longer
lets REPO-GIT-08 pass, and an organisation ruleset outside the collected
prefix is no longer read as absent.

The same rule applies to the recursive tree. A path missing from a truncated
tree is undecided rather than absent, so REPO-FILE-13, REPO-FILE-14, the
dual-licence scan, and every presence check report inconclusive instead of
drawing a conclusion from state they never received.

Collection members are now decoded strictly. A tree entry, tag, commit,
ruleset, or branch rule airlock cannot read is a malformed response, never
one fewer item — a malformed `.claude/config` entry used to disappear and
help REPO-FILE-13 pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: bind the issuer, budget the clock, and refuse ambiguous headers

Airlock Safe app user tokens are now bound to both halves of GitHub's issuer
attestation: the immutable app id 4409712 as well as the slug. A renamed app,
a reused slug, or an installation reporting app id zero or no app id at all
is refused rather than trusted.

Response headers are kept multi-valued. Two `X-OAuth-Scopes` fields have no
combination rule airlock is willing to invent, so a response carrying both a
read-only value and `repo` is refused whichever order they arrive in, and two
Link headers are a malformed response rather than a coin toss over which page
to fetch next.

Every request now carries connect and read timeouts, response bodies are read
under a byte cap rather than buffered whole, the recursive tree is checked
against the declared entry budget, and the whole run carries a wall-clock
deadline. The client takes all of these from the audit's Limits instead of
inventing private defaults. Policy bundles spend one aggregate byte budget
across the root and every reference, so a blob that would exceed it is
refused before it is fetched.

REPO-CI-04 now requires a version comment that names a version: a bare `#`,
a whitespace-only comment, and a `#` inside a quoted scalar no longer pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: close the three residual fail-open paths

A capability condition is now three-valued. `intentional-config-present`
asked `has_file`, which answers false for a path airlock never established
the absence of, so a truncated tree conclusively skipped every release rule
the registry capability governs. A condition whose input is truncated, over
budget, or unreadable now yields an inconclusive finding for each rule it
governs, and an audit that could not evaluate it is incomplete.

The device flow builds its own HTTP client, which had no timeouts at all —
so `auth login` and, through the refresh that runs before the bounded REST
client exists, `audit` and `auth status` could hang forever on a server that
accepted the connection and never answered. It now carries the same connect
and request timeouts as the audit path, reads bodies under a byte cap, and
bounds the whole poll loop to the lifetime of the device code it is polling
for.

Tag decoding no longer treats an unexpected ref as "simply not a tag". The
endpoint airlock asks is the refs/tags matching-ref collection, so a
refs/heads, refs/pull, or truncated refs/tag entry is malformed API data —
skipping it could empty a whole tag listing and let "no tag carries a `v`
prefix" pass over tags airlock never read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): report what each policy source pinned to, and read declarations whole

The bundle digest told a reviewer that the policy inputs changed without
telling them which reference changed, which is most of the value of pinning
reference data. Every source now carries its own resolved identity — commit
and blob sha for a remote source, content hash for a local one — through to
the findings document and the text renderer.

Sequences read out of files the audited repository controls are now read
strictly, through one shared helper. `topics: [cli, 42, rust]` used to yield
two topics: the count rule then failed a repository that declared three, and
the vocabulary rule never compared the dropped entry against the vocabulary
that would have rejected it. A wrong-typed entry is malformed input and the
rule reports it, in the same shape the GitHub client already uses for API
collections. The sweep covers topics, trigger lists, push branches, CD tag
patterns, renovate presets, branch-rule merge methods, hook commands, and the
policy's own topic vocabulary.

The text summary line is derived from the status taxonomy rather than
restating its eight members, so a ninth status cannot be added without the
renderer following.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cli): keep error causes and model credential selection truthfully

`main` prints `{error:#}`, which walks the source chain — but every core
error was being flattened into a fresh anyhow message first, so the chain it
walked was one link long. Each boundary now converts through `?` with a
`context` naming what airlock was trying to do, and the underlying cause
survives to the terminal.

Credential selection and credential origin were the same enum, which left a
`RefreshedProfile` arm that `selected_source` could never return and a match
arm nothing could reach. They are two enums now: selection is decided before
anything is read and cannot know whether a refresh will be needed.

The `AIRLOCK_TOKEN` name is read from its constant rather than respelled as a
literal, and a target that clap guarantees is present is no longer defaulted
into an empty string that reported "`` is not a repository".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* chore: point the topic vocabulary at its real home and tidy the manifests

The declared settings pointed readers at references/topics.md, a path left
over from the repository-standards template that does not exist here. The
vocabulary lives in the org policy's reference data.

AGENTS.md widened the no-shelling-out rule to "the tooling around it" and then
narrowed it to the binary, which reads as a standing violation by the
reconcile workflow. It is a rule about the binary; a workflow holding a scoped
token is exactly where a write belongs.

Both dev-dependency blocks restated tokio's features, which the workspace
already declares.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: read policy list parameters strictly and finish the error-cause sweep

`org-names: [wyrd-company, 42]` silently dropped an entry, so the rule that
forbids an organisation-name topic could pass while checking against a
shorter list than the policy declared. A list parameter that is not a list of
strings is now a malformed parameter the rule reports, naming the position of
the entry airlock could not read.

The last two boundaries in `auth login` were still flattening core errors
into fresh anyhow messages, dropping the source chain `main` prints, and one
test respelled AIRLOCK_TOKEN instead of using the constant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(core): make the two scope-header answers a type, and test the tree branch

`X-OAuth-Scopes` has three answers — absent, present-and-possibly-empty, and
repeated — and a Vec collapsed the first two into shapes a reader had to
decode, with a redundant boolean beside it that verification discarded. They
are an enum now, so each case is named where it is decided: an absent header
is an unread grant and refused, a present-but-empty header is GitHub stating
the token holds no scopes and is accepted, with the reasoning written where
the decision is made rather than inferred from a slice pattern.

The truncated-tree snapshot test reimplemented the production branch instead
of asserting through `file()`, so it passed whatever that branch did. It now
asserts through the accessor every check uses, in both directions; inverting
the branch fails four tests where it previously failed none.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: raise the minimum supported Rust version to 1.86

The dependency tree requires it: the icu_* crates that idna (via
reqwest's url) resolves to declare rustc 1.86, so a 1.85 toolchain
cannot even resolve the lockfile. Only CI's pinned MSRV job catches
this; the local msrv task runs on the installed toolchain.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: scope the msrv gate to what consumers build

The minimum supported Rust version is a promise about building airlock,
not about running its test suite; wiremock (dev-only) needs 1.88 without
declaring it, and it has no business setting the published floor. The
full suite still runs on stable in the test job.
